deed: שישה רופאים ואחים ישראלים סייעו לנפגעי רעידת אדמה בפרו
title: Israeli Medical Mission to Victims of the Earthquake in Peru

trailer.text: IsraAID, the Israel Forum for International Humanitarian Aid, and FIRST, an umbrella organization for Israeli emergency responder teams, initiated an Israeli medical mission to Peru.
An earthquake of magnitude 8 on the Richter scale struck Peru on August 15, and the city of Pisco was hit hardest.
Three Israeli doctors and three Israeli nurses were to fly there, meet with representatives of the Jewish community in Lima and continue to Pisco.
Dr. Ilya Geller, an orthopedic surgeon who volunteers with rescue units in the Galilee, said the mission would treat anyone who needs medical assistance.
At the same time, the Israeli embassy in Lima transferred medical equipment to the Peruvian authorities, and the Jewish community in Lima received tons of relief supplies.

glance.label: Support
glance.value: Bnei Brith and the American Jewish Committee

paragraphs.text: The earthquake struck Peru on 15 August at 18:40.
At its peak it reached a magnitude of 8 on the Richter scale.
It was also felt in Lima, the capital, where most of the Jewish community lives.
The town of Pisco was virtually destroyed.
In the towns of Ica and Chincha, many buildings were leveled.
Most of the houses that collapsed were older houses made of plaster-covered adobe bricks.
Pisco had about 130 thousand residents, and it was the hardest hit.
The mayor, Juan Mendoza, reported that 70% of the city's houses were destroyed.
According to him, communication lines and the water supply were cut off.
Hundreds of the dead were still lying in the streets or buried under the rubble.
Dozens of hungry survivors looted a central market in Pisco, and the humanitarian crisis worsened.
Many residents of the area fled in convoys of trucks and buses.
700 prisoners escaped from the local prison during the earthquake, and the police had difficulty locating them.
The UN and the European Union announced that they would provide aid amounting to one million dollars.
Doctors Without Borders planned to send a cargo plane from Bogota with five tons of medical and non-medical supplies.
Peru is a popular destination for Israeli trekkers, but no Israelis were known to be among the dead.
The Foreign Ministry succeeded in making contact with all the Israeli trekkers in Peru.
A spokeswoman for the Israeli Embassy in Lima said no Israeli citizens were known to have been killed or injured.
The Foreign Ministry in Jerusalem said $20,000 had been sent to the embassy in Lima to buy emergency provisions for victims.
According to Kol Yisrael, the money would be used to buy tents and blankets.
President Shimon Peres instructed diplomats to ask the Peruvians what further help Israel could offer.
He also instructed his military secretary to examine with the IDF ways to help Peru.
According to JTA, Israel has in the past organized major aid airlifts and search-and-rescue teams for disaster zones abroad.
The Israeli embassy in Lima transferred to the Peruvian authorities medical equipment donated by the Foreign Ministry.
It included antibiotics, painkillers, intravenous medications and bandages.
The equipment was flown in by military plane to the emergency logistics center in Pisco.
Embassy officials announced that Israel would also provide food and housing assistance.
The Israeli ambassador to Peru, Walid Manzur, arrived in Pisco to check on the progress of the rescue and aid efforts.
He said this was the fourth earthquake he had experienced, and that it was much stronger than the others.
Six Israeli medical personnel were to fly to Pisco on Monday night to help victims of the earthquake.
They were three doctors and three nurses.
The mission was initiated by FIRST, an umbrella organization for Israeli emergency responder teams, and IsraAID, the Israel Forum for International Humanitarian Aid.
It was supported by Bnei Brith and the Israeli branch of the American Jewish Committee.
The mission was to meet briefly in Lima with representatives of the Jewish community of Peru.
From there it was to travel to Pisco, one of the cities hit hardest.
Eran Lerman, head of the American Jewish Committee in Israel, said that helping countries and people struck by disaster is a Jewish and Zionist duty.
Dr. Ilya Geller is an orthopedic surgeon who volunteers with rescue units in the Galilee area.
This is his first volunteer mission outside of Israel.
Geller said that going to another country that has undergone a disaster in order to help people is a special and challenging mission.
According to him, the mission would get a vehicle that would serve as a supply base and drive around to help anyone in need.
Geller explained that in such natural disasters most of the injuries are broken and crushed bones or limbs.
Since many doctors in the area are not adequate in their capabilities, he said, the mission would treat anyone who needs medical assistance.
Nearly all of Peru's 3,000 Jews live in Lima.
According to John Gleiser, president of the Jewish Association of Peru, the community's response includes emergency aid and aid for long-term rebuilding.
By August 19, between three and four tons of relief supplies had arrived at the Jewish community in Lima.
The community's relief organizers used cash donations to buy thousands of blankets and more than 200 picks and shovels.
They decided to channel the aid through Caritas, the Catholic Church's humanitarian aid organization.

disagreements.question: How many people were killed in the earthquake?

versions.says: Head of the fire services, according to Walla!: at least 510 dead
Local sources cited by Doctors Without Borders: more than 500 dead
Head of the fire services, according to Walla!: 1,600 injured
Local sources cited by Doctors Without Borders: 1,000 injured

disagreements.question: How many people were left homeless?

versions.says: Walla!: about 80 thousand people lost family members or were left homeless
Jewish Journal: tens of thousands homeless

disagreements.question: How much medical equipment did Israel donate?

versions.says: ynetnews: the embassy transferred two tons of medical equipment donated by the Foreign Ministry
Jewish Journal: the Israeli government donated half a ton of medicines and medical supplies

disagreements.question: How far from Lima was the affected area?

versions.says: Walla!: the epicenter was about 150 km from Lima
Doctors Without Borders: the hardest-hit cities are about 200 km south of Lima

unknowns.text: The reports describe the mission before it set out; it is not known what it actually did in Pisco or how many people it treated
It is not known whether the inquiry ordered by President Peres led to further aid from Israel or from the IDF
